points.title: Tiafoe stages epic comeback to break Michelsen’s heart in US Open classic
points.content: No 11 seed rallies for 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (6) winTiafoe into third US Open semi-final in five yearsAmerican will play Alcaraz or Shelton in last fourAt the end of more than four and a half hours of escalating drama inside the world’s biggest tennis stadium, a devastated Alex Michelsen fell into Frances Tiafoe’s arms just outside the tramlines, sobbing uncontrollably. Tiafoe took his younger countryman in an embrace and held him there for 23 seconds, the victor consoling the vanquished in the aftermath of an extraordinary comeback that had carried him, somehow, into the US Open semi-finals.Only a couple of hours earlier, the 28-year-old Tiafoe had been two sets down and two points from elimination in the third set, with Michelsen within touching distance of the biggest victory of his young career. Instead, Tiafoe roared back from the brink to win a quarter-final that will be long remembered in New York, outlasting Michelsen 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (6) on Tuesday afternoon to reach the last four at Flushing Meadows for the third time in five years. Now he will face Ben Shelton on Friday after the American ousted defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in another epic five-set marathon that ended at 3.33am on Wednesday morning. Continue reading...

points.title: European democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyss | Rafael Behr
points.content: Far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin money are conniving to suffocate liberal idealism for another generationNot all that long ago, Europe was a beacon of liberal idealism. One memoir recalls it as an era “comfortably saturated with confidence in the unfailing and binding power of tolerance and conciliation”. The economic system seemed obviously preferable to barbarous alternatives. “People honestly believed that the divergencies and the boundaries between nations and sects would gradually melt away into a common humanity,” the author added.Those words could describe the spirit of globalisation at the turn of the millennium. They were written in the 1930s by Stefan Zweig, reflecting on the optimism of late 19th-century Vienna from the perspective of a Jewish émigré whose world had been destroyed by murderous nationalism. Zweig took his own life in 1942. He never saw fascism defeated. He couldn’t have imagined a renaissance of liberalism in the second half of the 20th century so complete as to attain a pitch of complacency rivalling the one he remembered from his childhood. points.title: ‘I fear the price could be high’: Inside the German state where the far-right surged
points.content: After the AfD’s landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt, people in the state capital share what they make of the result – and what comes next• Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereAsking residents in a city where a seismic political event has just taken place ‘How do you feel?’ demands chutzpah – this struck me as I walked around Magdeburg, Germany on Monday. The night before, the far-right populist, anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin party Alternative für Deustchland (AfD) had landslide 44% win in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections, sending shock waves to Berlin, across Germany and way beyond. Regardless of how people in the capital voted, it felt like a bit of an affront to probe. Given the radical plans of the victors, a party classified by domestic intelligence as “rightwing extremist”, that is what I wanted to know. But from the 21-year-old Guinean-German paramedic I met at the central bus station, collecting donations for a local hospice, to the elderly couple returning to their apartment after a stroll down the Elbe river, almost everyone I met opened up to me warmly.Judith, 88, was initially reluctant to talk, but shared some of her life story. Her experience as an eight-year-old refugee, forced to leave Poland in 1946 and eventually ending up move with her family in Magdeburg, had shaped her outlook on life, her successful career as a project engineer – as well as her politics. points.title: The Guardian view on Donald Trump’s oil deal: Venezuela pays for his vanity | Editorial
points.content: The US president seized a nation’s natural wealth in a modern-day version of gunboat diplomacy to feed his ego – not to lower Americans’ fuel billsImperialism does not require a flag to be planted or a governor dispatched. It can be a powerful nation deciding who governs a smaller, weaker country, and on what terms and for whose benefit its resources will be developed. Donald Trump’s kidnapping of Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro, putting his deputy – Delcy Rodríguez – in his place as president, and then her signing a deal handing a fifth of the country’s proven oil reserves to the US, amount to a modern version of 19th-century gunboat diplomacy. Regime change supplied America’s commercial concession.This won’t bother Mr Trump. But it should. The US president has oversold his neocolonial spoils. The additional production Venezuela is supposed to bring online might bring down oil prices eventually, but not anytime soon. Crucially, what Mr Trump calls “the biggest oil deal in history” won’t cause the price at the pump to fall before November’s midterms. When so many American voters are struggling to pay energy bills, it’s hard to see how unrealised Orinoco Belt riches are going to help Republican candidates.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? points.title: Scientists find a bone-building switch that could fight osteoporosis
points.content: An experimental compound called AP503 significantly strengthened bones in mice by activating GPR133, a receptor that boosts bone formation while slowing bone loss. Because the same treatment has also been linked to stronger muscles, researchers see intriguing potential for combating age-related decline and osteoporosis.

points.title: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS is bursting with methanol
points.content: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS contains exceptionally high levels of methanol, suggesting it formed under conditions very different from those that shaped most comets in our solar system. ALMA also revealed that tiny icy grains around the comet are releasing methanol like miniature comets, giving astronomers an unusually detailed look at an object from another star system.

points.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
points.content: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

points.title: Ozempic and Wegovy linked to nearly 40% fewer asthma attacks
points.content: Semaglutide, the drug found in Ozempic and Wegovy, was linked to nearly 40% fewer asthma attacks in a large real-world study. It was also associated with about 20% fewer COPD flare-ups. Researchers say GLP-1 drugs may offer respiratory benefits in addition to their effects on diabetes and obesity, but clinical trials are needed to confirm the findings.

points.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
points.content: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

points.title: Chinese scientists find a hidden atomic structure that unlocks methane
points.content: Scientists found that a tiny atomic structure that forms on nickel oxide during methane conversion is more effective than the metallic nickel long believed to drive the reaction. The discovery allowed a low-nickel catalyst to rival one containing 10 times more metal, potentially opening the door to cheaper and more efficient industrial catalysts.

points.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
points.content: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

points.title: Caffeine may flip an ancient cellular switch linked to slower aging
points.content: Scientists found that caffeine activates an ancient cellular energy system involved in stress resistance, DNA repair, and growth. The discovery could help explain caffeine’s links to healthier aging and may point toward new ways to target the same pathway.

points.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
points.content: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

points.title: Dark energy debunked? Cosmic acceleration may be an illusion
points.content: A new analysis of more than 1,700 supernovae is questioning whether the universe is really accelerating at all. After accounting for the ages of the stars that produce these explosions, researchers found signs that cosmic expansion may actually be slowing. They also argue that the apparent acceleration changes with direction, which would be difficult to explain with dark energy. Other cosmologists dispute the conclusion, setting up a major test for upcoming observatories.

points.title: Astronomers detect ancient hydrogen signal that could help map the Universe
points.content: Astronomers have detected an exceptionally faint hydrogen radio signal from billions of light-years away using South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope. Instead of finding galaxies one at a time, the technique measures their combined hydrogen glow across enormous stretches of space. The successful detection shows that astronomers may soon be able to create much larger 3D maps of the Universe.

points.title: Why our common ancestor with chimpanzees keeps getting further away
points.content: The more we learn about chimpanzees, the more they resemble us – but the further back in time our shared ancestor seems to be. Columnist Michael Marshall explores how both can be true

points.title: Bursts of ‘pink noise’ during sleep seem to help clear waste from brain
points.content: The human brain flushes out waste products while we sleep and now it seems that certain sounds might enhance the process

points.title: Heat spikes over Tibet may help explain severe Californian flooding
points.content: Unusually high temperatures over the mountainous region can kick-start a chain of events that ultimately leads to a severe deluge on the US West Coast, scientists say

points.title: Earliest evidence of habitual drug use found in teeth in Indonesia
points.content: Strange, rounded grooves in prehistoric teeth are thought to have been made by regularly sucking whole betel nuts to extract a pain-relieving compound. This marks the earliest known example of probable substance addiction

points.title: Unexpected hints of dark matter should breathe life into particle physics
points.content: With little in the way of significant discoveries since 2012, there have been mutterings that particle physics is at a dead end. However, new dark matter results suggest an exciting new way to hunt for reality's undiscovered ingredients

points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02843-4Evidence suggests that regular calls can keep kids learning when schooling is disrupted — plus, why a familiar world map may be about to change.

points.title: Bacteria recruited to treat cancer
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02823-8Anticancer drugs could be manufactured and delivered by modified microorganisms.

points.title: Breaking timescales with generative sampling of conformational transitions
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11025-1A generative committor-guided path-sampling framework reconstructs rare biomolecular transition pathways and reveals the underlying thermodynamics and kinetics without using predefined collective variables or brute-force sampling, at an acceptable computational cost.

points.title: Within-family effect of ancestry on complex traits in a Mexican population
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11039-9This study uses a within-family design to identify significant ancestry differences in complex traits such as height and type 2 diabetes in a genetically diverse population from Mexico City.

points.title: Neocortical long-range inhibition promotes cortical synchrony and sleep
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10876-yIn mice, a sparse population of sleep-active long-range inhibitory neurons in the neocortex promote widespread cortical synchronization and sleep, revealing a cortical mechanism that contributes to the regulation of sleep.

points.title: An operational perturbation proteomics-based virtual cell model
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11001-9Temporal protein-abundance measurements from systematically perturbed breast cancer cell lines were generated to develop ProteinTalks, a virtual cell model that functions as an operational tool for diverse drug discovery tasks.

points.title: PLA2G2D in tumour-draining lymph nodes regulates anti-tumour immunity
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10954-1A specific population of macrophages that express high levels of the enzyme PLA2G2D in tumour-draining lymph nodes is associated with poor prognosis in patients, and inhibiting PLA2G2D improves anti-tumour immunity in mouse models.

points.title: Foaming photopolymers as a high-resolution biomimetic printing platform
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10968-9Deep-foam photolithography uses light-controlled polymer foaming to create high-resolution, multifunctional microstructures with tunable optical, wetting and fluid-handling properties for advanced manufacturing applications.

points.title: Advancing conflict research and response through satellite-derived data
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11004-6Integrating satellite-derived war-damage data with text-based fatality records through improvement, enrichment and fusion mitigates limitations inherent in each source, revealing complex violence dynamics beyond fatality-centric paradigms, as case studies from Ukraine and Myanmar illustrate.

points.title: Denisovans from southwestern China and their subsistence strategies
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10997-4Evidence from Bianfu Cave shows specialized hunting, expedient stone-tool production and extensive bone use of Denisovans, providing new insights into their ecology, behaviour and cultural legacy in eastern Asia.

points.title: A serpin–myeloid axis in pancreatic cancer heterogeneity and immune evasion
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11002-8SERPINE1 and SERPINB2-driven fibrin-rich niches locally programme immunosuppressive macrophages and exclude T cells, enabling spatially organized immune evasion in pancreatic ductal carcinoma.

points.title: Mobile education builds resilience during shocks in five countries
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10990-xRemote phone-based targeted tutoring in five countries produced large, cost-effective learning gains during school closures, outperforming text messaging and working effectively when delivered by governments or non-governmental organizations to strengthen education resilience.

points.title: Ancient proteins identify various Denisovan remains from Southwest China
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10976-9Identification and proteomic analysis of bone fragments and teeth from an excavation in Southwest China provide insight into the evolution and phenotype of Denisovans and fill a geographical gap in their documented distribution.

points.title: Predicting genome-wide functional constraints with GPN-Star
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11005-5GPN-Star, a genomic language model with a phylogeny-aware architecture for whole-genome alignment data, is shown to be a scalable and flexible tool for genetic variant effect prediction across species.

points.title: Imaging cellular activity across all organs reveals body-wide circuits
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10979-6An imaging system developed to record cellular activity throughout the whole body of zebrafish captures cellular organ dynamics and identifies multiple distributed circuits.

points.title: TRI-611, a selective, brain-penetrant molecular glue degrader of ALK
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10998-3TRI-611 induces the degradation of ALK fusion proteins via a previously undescribed CRBN recruitment motif, and its preclinical anti-tumour activity highlights TRI-611 as a potential new way of treating ALK-positive non-small-cell lung cancer.

points.title: Anodic Pd membrane H2 extraction enhances thermochemical dehydrogenation
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11008-2An electrochemical cell with molten hydroxide and a Pd membrane actively extracts H2 and thereby boosts ammonia and methylcyclohexane conversion, while also delivering purified H2 ready for use.

points.title: Integrated signatures define mutational processes in prostate cancer
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10468-wEight integrated mutational footprints collectively explain the mutational processes in 85% of primary prostate cancer genomes.

points.title: TM184C is a GPCR-like regulator of intercellular exchange and autophagy
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10993-8TM184C—an ancient G-protein-coupled receptor-like superdark protein involved in regulation of autophagy, intercellular connectivity and material exchange—underscores the promise of exploring the understudied human proteome and beyond.

points.title: Proximity-guided graph learning reveals tumour-associated proximity antigens
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11003-7A proximity-mapping atlas defines tumour-associated proximity antigens, revealing disease-associated membrane spatial communities, and identifies EGFR–CDCP1 as a co-target pair that enhances tumour killing by multispecific therapeutics.

points.title: In the basement of miniaturized relics
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02416-5Thinking small.

points.title: AI model predicts which breast-cancer drugs work best
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02845-2Model trained on millions of protein measurements can gauge drug effectiveness in tissue samples taken from people with triple-negative breast cancer.

points.title: These six advances could change how drugs are delivered
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02654-7Medication triggered by your circadian clock, self-assembling delivery systems based on DNA and other highlights from studies and trials.

points.title: DNA-editing ‘pencils’ probe early human development
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02840-7A genome-rewriting approach known as adenine base editing offers a precise way to investigate gene function in early human embryos.

points.title: Popular open-science platform to stop hosting data and code amid funding concerns
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02598-yChanges to the Open Science Framework’s policies will come into effect in November, forcing researchers to reconsider their workflows.

points.title: Special delivery: bacterial couriers are smuggling drugs into cancers
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02657-4Microorganisms that deliver treatments to tumours could make chemotherapy, radiotherapy and immunotherapy safer and more effective.

points.title: Uniform film formation helps tandem solar cells work better for longer
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02709-9When making mixed-halide perovskite films for use in solar cells, bromide-rich domains crystallize faster than iodide-rich ones do, leading to defects. Adding a molecule tuned to bind selectively to bromide-bound lead synchronizes the crystallization rates, yielding uniform films, better operating stability and a more-efficient perovskite–organic tandem.

points.title: Use AI as a sparring partner, not an oracle
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02846-1As artificial-intelligence tools become crucial collaborators in science, universities must teach students to challenge such systems and assess their ability to do so.

points.title: Who were the Denisovans? Rich trove of fossils and tools paints new picture
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02810-zObjects found in a cave in southwestern China suggest that these enigmatic ancient humans were accomplished hunters.

points.title: Combined satellite and news data capture unseen aspects of war
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02523-3Records of war extracted from news reports have shaped what researchers know about violence. Satellite images could transform that understanding — if access stays open.

points.title: Drug-delivering particles aim to breach the blood–brain barrier
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02655-6The inability to get drugs into the brain has impeded the treatment of cancer and neurodegenerative diseases for decades. Techniques based on nanoparticles and exosomes are vying to provide a solution.

points.title: Phone-based tutoring improves learning during school closures
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02471-yOne-to-one phone sessions substantially increased students’ numeracy test scores in low- and middle-income countries that experience emergencies that disrupt schooling.

points.title: Medicines do no good if people don’t take them
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02658-3Health psychologist Rob Horne explains why medication non-adherence is such a problem, and how behavioural science can help to address it.

points.title: Hello Equal Earth: what the UN’s new world map will change
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02820-xWhat the UN vote to ditch the Mercator projection means for education, navigation and public perception.

points.title: Pick up the phone! Phone calls with tutors keep kids learning when schools shut down
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02825-6The low-cost intervention was trialled in five countries during the COVID-19 pandemic.

points.title: Phone-call tutorials improve learning cost-effectively during education emergencies
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02700-4Across five randomized trials in India, Kenya, Nepal, the Philippines and Uganda, weekly 20-minute mobile-phone-call tutorials produced large learning gains for primary-school children during school closures caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Governments can keep children learning through societal shocks using this approach, which combines low-cost, high-access mobile-phone technology with high-quality tutoring targeted to each child’s learning level.

points.title: A good drug is useless if it misses its target
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02653-8The best medicines go exactly where they’re needed in the body— and nowhere else.

points.title: Electric charge makes drops of water more destructive
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02705-zIn many real-world settings, water droplets can become slightly charged as they slide across solid surfaces. This charge has been found to enable water droplets to damage protective coatings more easily than uncharged droplets do, and to cause the underlying metal to corrode.

points.title: Family-based analyses show how children’s genetics shape key traits
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02689-wThe Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study, called MoBa, includes genetic data from around 230,000 parents and children. Using about 44,000 father–mother–child trios, child and parental genetics were modelled together to estimate the effects of the children’s own genetic differences on their height, educational achievement, sleep duration and depressive symptoms.

points.title: Genetic associations with the Big Five personality traits probed in one million people
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02790-0Human DNA has been linked to personality traits — how individuals think, feel and act — thus identifying hundreds of genetic variants that contribute to the traits’ moderate heritability. The pathways from DNA to personality are robust yet complex, with widespread relevance for health, wealth, work and love.

points.title: Dose once, treat forever: drugs are being engineered to last much longer
points.content: Nature, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02660-9Medication that persists inside the body for months or years could transform the treatment and prevention of many conditions — especially in low- and middle-income countries.

points.title: Nasal vaccines could stop pandemics before they begin

points.title: Tuesday briefing: What happens next after Germany’s far-right breakthrough?
points.content: In today’s newsletter: The AfD’s local election triumph has shocked Europe, and raised questions about how to counter the rising far rightGood morning. Across Germany – and Europe more widely – there has been a palpable sense of shock and disbelief after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) swept to a historic state election victory in the early hours of Monday.It was, according to France’s European affairs minister, Benjamin Haddad, “a very grave moment for Europe”. It’s a very different story for the 49ers: facing Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett, not to mention the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks, at least twice this season is the least of their problems. Ali explores how attacks on Muslims by successive administrations since 9/11 cemented Islamophobia in all areas of American life, and she explains why she believes these prejudices are more pervasive now than ever. points.title: America: the gulf, the lake and now the state – what’s next on Trump’s huge renaming spree? | Marina Hyde
points.content: Farewell, New Mexico. The war isn’t going well and nowhere on Earth is safe from the US president’s favourite displacement activityBusy times for crayon-wielding US president Donald Trump, Earth’s most tireless freelance cartographer, who at the weekend celebrated the US labouring under the highest diesel prices in its history while his “two-week” Iran war edges into its seventh month with a social media spree in which he pushed renaming New Mexico as New America.In some ways, it was a surprise to see Trump go for merely rebranding a state at this point, given that it was only so recently that he declared: “If you think about it, we have a gulf, and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean.” This is believed to be a reference to the Gulf of America, formerly – and indeed currently, in every meaningful sense – the Gulf of Mexico. It was also a nod to Lake America, as precisely no one calls Lake Ontario despite Trump supposedly retitling it by executive order last month, in another fit of pique over his trade war with Canada. Candidates for this heavily trailed American Ocean clearly include the Pacific and the Atlantic – though why the other oceans should be locationally ineligible increasingly feels unclear. At this rate, geography exams in the US are also about to get a whole lot easier.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnistWhat a Time to be Alive! by Marina Hyde (Guardian Faber Publishing, £20). To support the Guardian, order your signed copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply. Continue reading...

points.title: Trump’s approval rating is plummeting – as his fortune grows and grows | Arwa Mahdawi
points.content: The US president says criticising his soaring investment portfolio is ‘very unfair’. Tell that to the millions of Americans struggling with the cost of livingIf I had a dollar for every time Donald Trump said something inane, I would be a very rich woman. But even with an income that steady, I could never hope to be as flush as the president. A Forbes calculation from March puts his net worth at about $6.5bn – and it’s growing rapidly. Trump made $2.2bn in 2025 via business interests that ranged from selling cryptocurrency and Trump Bibles to offering early access to his (often market-moving) Truth Social posts.To be fair, Trump isn’t making all this money just so he can buy golf clubs and gold toilets. No, he’s amassing these billions for the good of the little people; it’s altruism, not avarice! “I do this for our Country, not myself,” the president wrote on Truth Social on Sunday night alongside an AI-generated picture of him trading Intel stock. “I’ve made Hundreds of Billions of Dollars on Stocks, and many other type Holdings, for the U.S.A., not myself, and all I do is get criticized by the Radical Left Dumocrats. Very unfair, but what can you do!” Continue reading...

points.title: MLS’s transfer window and the spending line that keeps going up
points.content: Summer spending across the league’s 30 clubs has ballooned. Here are three takeaways from the league’s transfer windowWith the shadow of the 2026 World Cup hanging over the league and a potential set of rule changes looming, Major League Soccer’s summer transfer window was one defined by uncertainty, diverse strategies and record spending. It was the fourth transfer window since MLS allowed clubs to purchase players from other clubs using traditional transfer fees rather than general allocation money (GAM), the intraleague currency system. The new rule, which is now being used more frequently, has helped account for rapid growth in league expenditure, as has increased GAM allotted to each club.These trends have been seen broadly over the last two seasons, but this past window took it to a new level, smashing the previous record for summer spending. This summer, MLS teams spent 65% more year-over-year, with a total of nearly $190m spent, accounting for 45% of the 2026 total. The above factors combined to create one of the most consequential transfer windows in MLS history, which may give a glimpse into the league’s future trajectory. Continue reading...

points.title: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
points.content: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heatTyphoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people.Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing. Continue reading...

points.title: Elon Musk thanked by German far-right leader after landmark election win praised by Russia | First Thing
points.content: Populist, far-right, anti-immigration AfD wins vote in eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. Plus, 50 years since The Muppet Show first hit our screensDon’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up hereGood morning. A far-right leader who has won an important state election in Germany has thanked Elon Musk for his support, as voices in Europe warn the result is a serious moment for the continent. No far-right party has led or formed a government in Germany since the defeat of nazism at the end of the second world war.Ulrich Siegmund, the Alternative für Deutschland’s lead candidate, thanked Musk on X after the tech billionaire said “Well done!” in German to the AfD co-founder Alice Weidel. The populist, far-right, anti-immigration party won the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.Will the AfD be able to form a state government? Despite its resounding victory, the party fell just short of a majority. It was seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern alone and overcome the so-called “firewall” of the mainstream parties, which refuse to work with it. The final results showed the AfD falling three seats short, with 39 lawmakers in an 83-member legislature.What has been the reaction in Washington and Moscow? Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the election projection without comment on his Truth Social site. The Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump’s post and praised a “historic win for the pragmatic AfD”. The AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians in Germany to no longer receive refugee status.Who else has been saying Trump’s war may not achieve its aims? The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, said on Sunday morning Washington might not be able to reach an agreement with Tehran that would prevent Iran from having nuclear weapons. “We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said. Continue reading...

points.title: ‘The most anti-union president’: how Trump turned his back on US workers
points.content: Labor experts stunned at how anti-worker Trump has been with actions since last Labor Day that have hurt unionsDonald Trump has repeatedly vowed to champion US workers. Shortly before Labor Day last year, he said: “Every policy of the Trump administration is designed to lift up the American worker and “promote great-paying blue-collar jobs”. But in the year since last Labor Day, Trump has taken many actions that have hurt US workers and unions, with some labor experts saying they’ve been stunned at how anti-worker Trump has been.In the months after Trump returned to office, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) cut workplace inspections by 20%, compared with Joe Biden’s last year in office. Even though Trump campaigned as a champion of coal miners, his administration has repeatedly delayed implementation of a rule to limit silica dust, which has afflicted and killed many coal miners with black lung. The United Mine Workers union has urgently called for “immediate enforcement” of the stalled silica dust rule. Continue reading...

points.title: 25 years ago, two strangers met in the twin towers and escaped on 9/11. What happened next?
points.content: Stanley Primnath and Brian Clark were two of only four individuals known to have survived above the impact zone in the north towerHe has told the story hundreds of times, but it never seems to fade. If anything, it only becomes more vivid. “Oh, gosh,” exclaims Stanley Praimnath, his voice cracking with an “ooooooh!” as if bearing a weight. “It’s like reliving that day.”Nearly 3,000 people died in the terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DC on September 11 2001. But Praimnath and another office worker, Brian Clark, were two of only four individuals known to have survived from above the impact zone in either tower of the World Trade Center. The two strangers met in the smoke and fire of the 81st floor of the south tower, and walked down 1,620 steps into the rest of their lives. Continue reading...

points.title: Lindsay Clancy’s case is a Rorschach test | Moira Donegan
points.content: Clancy’s case became a referendum on mothers, healthcare and the status of womenMost family annihilators are men. It’s a grim fact that such incidents are common enough to have a discernible pattern. The massacre is carried out by a husband and father, often one who is on the verge of bankruptcy or divorce; typically, it forms the finale of a long reign of domestic violence terror.About half the time, the perpetrator kills himself after slaughtering his family. Gun use is common – a large number of what are termed “mass shootings” in the United States are in fact family annihilation killings, in which a man turns his weapon on his family members. Other times, the killer uses knives, or fires. Continue reading...

points.title: For baseball’s Black and Latino players, it’s always 1926 somewhere
points.content: From home-run celebrations to tilted caps, players embracing joy continue to collide with an old guard devoted to Dust Bowl grimnessOver the last several years, simultaneously lauded and paralyzed by its ironclad traditions, baseball has undergone various forays into reinvention, trying to free itself from its unwritten rules of retaliation, its seeming aversion to joy, its demand that every generation of player of every culture and background play the game with the grimness of a Dust Bowl farmer.The sport even attempted to change those customs by promoting a cultural shift with an industry-wide motto: Let the Kids Play. But in a time of intense division within the aggressive backdrop of Trumpism, the result is a racial clash that is actually a generational and cultural one that predates current politics by a century.Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including Full Dissidence: Notes from an Uneven Playing Field, and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America. He writes at Substack. Continue reading...

points.title: Will hordes of influencers, weed smokers and mid-point talkers bring down the US Open?
points.content: This year, the noise at the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center has officially become A Problem. But changing it would mean changing societyThe first thing you notice while sitting in the upper tiers of Arthur Ashe Stadium is the noise. A persistent exterior hum filters up from ground level, fed by the massive ventilation and cooling units that sit outside the stadium, the clack of the Long Island Rail Road to the north, and the forklifts receiving goods from the refrigerator trucks that keep the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center flush with its essential supplies of Evian, champagne, and premium IPA. Overhead, planes descending toward LaGuardia airport ensure the auditory assault takes place by land and air simultaneously. In the lower rakes of the stadium, the babble of the spectators is incessant; it’s not unusual to overhear full-volume conversations on various non-tennis topics – work, family, romance, last night’s dinner – that continue without interruption for the duration of an entire match.New York is famously noisy, and the US Open, as the most glamorous annual sporting event in town, has always been loud in sympathy with its environment. Indeed, the brashness of the American grand slam has historically been its major selling point, the signature that distinguishes it from the Australian Open (the “happy slam”), Wimbledon (strawberries and cream, all-white attire, the home of tennis), and the French Open (French). People have been complaining about the volume of the New York crowd for decades. But this year the noise at the US Open feels different. This year noise at the noisy slam has become A Problem. points.title: Europe’s centre fears nationalist wave after AfD victory but only has itself to blame

points.title: The world is being driven to the brink by thugs and dictators, but there is a route to a brighter future | Simon Tisdall
points.content: It’s no surprise some analysts say we are already in the midst of the third world war, but ordinary people have more power than we think Don’t look up! The world is a mess. The sky could fall in any day. Unending wars, expanding humanitarian crises, rising authoritarianism, dysfunctional democracies, rampant racial and religious extremism, and unchecked lawlessness cast a dark cloud as the west’s new political year begins. Set all that against a backdrop of staggering global economic inequality, corporate and individual greed, irresponsible government indebtedness, dangerous AI gambles, climate breakdown and proliferating nuclear weapons, and a truly apocalyptic global outlook begins to take shape. It’s enough to make anyone shut their eyes, cover their ears and utter a Munch-like scream. And it’s only getting worse.Democratic leaders who promise a better, safer, more optimistic future – what Britain’s freshly arrived prime minister, Andy Burnham, calls a “new era of possibility” – cannot escape this wider international context. Last week’s global bond market upheaval, sparked by external factors, left Burnham’s cash-strapped government struggling with sharply increased borrowing costs before he barely got started. The fact he chose Ukraine for his first overseas trip, while symbolically important, highlighted another grim reality. As a lead opponent of Vladimir Putin’s invasion, Britain now finds itself in a de facto state of war with Russia – and facing attack. Argentina, too, is eyeing UK defence vulnerabilities. These are not the sort of possibilities Burnham envisaged. Continue reading...

points.title: That sound you hear is not the world ending – it’s liberalism being monstered | Waleed Aly
points.content: It turns out most of us no longer believe in progress. And when that happens, it quickly becomes a crisis for societies like oursGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastDepending on your politics, the monsters are everywhere. Perhaps you see them in the form of tech billionaires and the artificial intelligence they’re developing. Perhaps you see them in the bin fire of social media they bequeathed us before that, or the legacy media that refuse to tell you “the truth”. You might see them in the manosphere, or the institutions teaching our kids gender fluidity. Maybe you see them in the migrant youth wielding machetes in the suburbs, or the refugee attempting to behead someone on a Belfast street. Or perhaps you see them in the violent anti-immigrant mobs that torched houses in response. If so, you’ll likely see them in the March for Australia or the Unite the Kingdom rallies, organised by far-right groups but attended by many more besides. You’ll almost certainly see them in at least one of Hamas, Israel or those local advocates at each other’s throats over the Middle East. I suspect you’ll see them in Russia but that can no longer be assumed. And I’d guess that you’d see them in at least one political party with a significant share of the vote.Something in that paragraph probably outraged you. In which case, you’re probably seeing monsters in whoever sees different monsters from you. It would be easy here to make a point about polarisation. But I want to look at the deep disquiet that lies underneath. Continue reading...

points.title: US overcome poor shooting and Italy’s eye-poke claims in edgy Fiba World Cup win
points.content: USA edge into quarter’s with nervy 55-52 winCecilia Zandalasini claims she was poked in eyeCaitlin Clark shoots 0-6 from the fieldJackie Young had a big fourth quarter and Breanna Stewart made her only basket of the game to put ⁠the United States up for good, helping the Americans escape with a 55-52 win over Italy in the Fiba Women’s World ⁠Cup on Sunday.The ​US (2-0), who clinched a quarter-final berth with the victory, led only 42-39 after three quarters and fell behind by two points on three occasions in the fourth. Stewart’s jumper, assisted by Young, gave the Americans a 51-50 lead with 3:20 to go, and Young hit a ⁠floater on their next possession. Chelsea Gray made a pull-up with 1:07 left for an ​important cushion, but Italy hit a quick ‌two-pointer in response to ‌cut it to 55-52. Gray missed a shot on the next US trip but Young ‌corralled the rebound to help her team bleed more clock. Continue reading...

points.title: Popular brain supplement linked to shorter lifespan in men
points.content: A large study involving more than 270,000 people has linked higher blood levels of the amino acid tyrosine to a shorter lifespan in men. Using both observational data and genetic analysis, researchers found that elevated tyrosine could potentially reduce male life expectancy by nearly a year, while no significant effect appeared in women. Tyrosine is found naturally in protein-rich foods and is also sold as a supplement for boosting focus and mental performance, making the finding especially intriguing.

points.title: The US attorney general is fretting about a ‘pandemic’ of gender transitions in schools | Arwa Mahdawi
points.content: Todd Blanche’s remarks are part of a totally-not-invented moral panic that stretches the limits of the imaginationBeing a public school teacher in the US these days is tough. You’ve got to pay for a lot of your own supplies, deal with smartphone-addicted children and perform gender-affirming surgeries on your lunch break.Luckily our intrepid attorney general, Todd Blanche, is on the case. Blanche appeared on Fox News this week to decry a “pandemic” of gender transitions in schools across the US. “There’s not a parent in America, no matter where you live, that would want their school to change and call their child by a different name and not expect to be told about that. We partnered with the Department of Education recently to combat this very trend and, really, pandemic that’s happening in some school districts around the country,” Blanche said. He seemed more concerned with name changes than with surgery, but the president himself has suggested on several occasions that schools are furtively doing surgery on children. During a campaign speech in 2024, for example, Donald Trump said: “Can you imagine … your son leaves the house and you say: ‘Jimmy, I love you so much. Go have a good day in school,’ and your son comes back with a brutal operation? Can you even imagine this?”Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

points.title: CTE in football players is a health crisis. It’s time for us to stop watching
points.content: A new study offers more evidence that America’s biggest sport produces life-altering head trauma. The NFL will never turn itself off, so it’s on fans to do soAs a new NFL season begins this Wednesday, the danger of America’s most-watched sport has never been more clear.A new and widely circulated study published in the British Medical Journal examined the donated brains of former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 and compared them with the overall number of players who died during that period. Of the 235 donated brains in that period, 215 had evidence of the degenerative brain condition chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). That group of 215 comprised 24.5% of the former players who died during that period in total. Given the finding, the study’s authors estimate that the prevalence of CTE among players who died in that period was at minimum 24.5% to a maximum of 97.7%, with the actual rate likely somewhere in between.Nathan Kalman-Lamb is Associate Professor of Sociology at the University of New Brunswick. Derek Silva is Associate Professor of Sociology and Criminology at King’s University College at Western University.In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123, or email jo@samaritans.org or jo@samaritans.ie. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org Continue reading...

(Source: Bloomberg)

points.title: US Strikes Iranian Tankers After Attack on US Warships

points.title: Esper Raises Concern Over Pentagon Leadership Loss

points.title: EU Envoy Urges Maximum Pressure on Russia

points.title: By The Way: Headlines You Should See

points.title: Thieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soar

points.title: The wild world of LSU: from tigers on the field to wooing ex-NFL players
points.content: Recruiting ex-pros. Inflaming Ukraine-Russia tensions. Suing the SEC and being sued back. The school is adapting to a new reality – and also creating a new oneIn 1893, a chemistry professor named Charles Coates arrived at Louisiana State University and wrote that, to his surprise, “there was practically no athletics in the student body: no football, no tennis, and only very little baseball in the spring.” A broad program of sports struck him as the kind of thing a school should have, particularly as US universities were beginning to tout intercollegiate athletics as critical to a balanced higher-ed experience and another way to justify the cost of entry. But 133 years on, sports aren’t merely the main attraction at LSU. They’re the school’s raison d’être, the blinkered obsession that consumes the university and its most prominent ambassadors.Any doubt that the business of educating college students is just a nettlesome distraction from the business of college sports in Baton Rouge has been emphatically dispelled over the past 10 months. On the football side, the school has spent or committed roughly $162m to its last three head coaches: Ed Orgeron, the folksy national champion in 2019 who received a $17m buyout when he was fired two years later; Brian Kelly, the unloved underachiever who received a $54m buyout after being fired last October; and Lane Kiffin, the Kelly replacement whom it signed to a $91m deal a month later. Clemson, the opponent for LSU’s season opener at home on Saturday, are about to find out what all that money buys. Continue reading...

points.title: Andy Ruiz Jr once turned boxing upside down. Can he do it again at 36?
points.content: Seven years after springing one of the biggest upsets in boxing history, the Mexican Rocky is back with his old trainer for one final run at the heavyweight summitSeven years ago, Andy Ruiz Jr became the first fighter of Mexican descent to win the world heavyweight championship in one of the biggest upsets boxing has ever seen, stopping the undefeated Anthony Joshua inside seven rounds at Madison Square Garden.A replacement opponent summoned on five weeks’ notice who went off as an 11-1 underdog, Ruiz came off the canvas in the third to knock Joshua down four times before the referee finally waved it off. Hailed as the “Mexican Rocky”, he was lionized as a border-straddling hero in his hometown of Imperial, the dusty agricultural community framed by the mountain ranges and flat deserts of south-eastern California. He made the late-night rounds, took an audience with Mexico president Andrés Manuel López Obrador and signed a $10m guarantee when Joshua activated his rematch clause. The money, cars, fame and women arrived all at once. Continue reading...

points.title: Why Laser Beams Are the Hottest New Tech in Defense
points.content: Our guest today is Colonel Sanders. More precisely, we speak with Wayne Sanders, a retired US army colonel who is currently senior defense research analyst for Bloomberg Intelligence. During his military career, Sanders specialized in cybersecurity and weapon systems research and his work for BI has recently focused on directed energy weapon systems — better known as lasers. Just a few decades ago, programs like Star Wars, the Reagan-era missile defense system, seemed like a pipedream; today lasers can shoot down missiles and much more. Sanders tells us about the physics problems researchers had to solve to make laser weapons a reality, why we still don't have laser guns, what makes a weapons system "exquisite," the economic costs that factor into battlefield decisions, and the unique supply chain constraints that affect laser development. points.title: Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy murder case after jury fails to reach unanimous verdict – as it happened
points.content: This blog is now closed. You can find more of our reporting on the mistrial of Massachusetts mother who killed her three children here:Full report: Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy caseExplained: Lindsay Clancy mistrial – what happens next?Five key moments from ‘America’s saddest murder trial’If you’re just joining us, the judge in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three young children, plans to declare a mistrial after the jury could not reach a unanimous verdict and remained deadlocked after a week of deliberations.Jurors in Plymouth state court spent more than 38 hours in deliberations over the charges against the 36-year-old mom, which came on the heels of a weeks-long trial that directed national attention to maternal mental health issues that can occur postpartum.Closing arguments ended last Thursday in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother who admitted killing her three young children – Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months – in January 2023. Her attempt to kill herself after killing the children left her with spinal injuries that paralyzed her from the waist down. Clancy pleaded not guilty to three counts of first-degree murder due to lack of criminal responsibility, also known as an insanity defense. She faced life in prison if convicted. The tragic case has sparked a national conversation about the state of postpartum mental healthcare in the United States.The charges up for consideration were first-degree murder, which involves “deliberate premeditation” or “extreme atrocity or cruelty” and is punishable by life in prison without the possibility of parole, or second-degree murder, without either of those conditions, punishable by life in prison with the possibility of parole. They also considered lesser manslaughter charges, which is punishable by up to 20 years in prison. If they had found Clancy not guilty, she could have spent the rest of her life in hospital, with the eventual possibility of release at a later time if the court determined she was not a danger to others.Jurors began deliberating last Thursday on whether to accept her insanity defense, but, almost 40 hours on, they have now declared three times that they could not reach a unanimous decision. A jury note indicated that jurors were split 11-1 toward an acquittal but a holdout juror “has acknowledged doubt but refuses to apply it to the verdict”. The prosecution argued this indicated a disagreement among jurors over how to weigh the evidence, while the defense argued the juror had “lied” when they swore to the judge to properly follow the law. But the judge ultimately declined to question the juror further or have them removed.After the jury declared today that, “with a heavy heart”, it still cannot “and will not be able to” reach a verdict, the judge said he intends to declare a mistrial. That has now been thrown into limbo after the defense asked for an emergency stay from Massachusetts’s highest court. The judge gave him one hour. We’ll bring you the latest as that unfolds.At the heart of what has been called America’s saddest murder trial is Clancy’s mental health following the birth of her third child. Her defense, led by attorney Kevin Reddington, argued that Clancy should not be held criminally responsible for killing her children because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis – a devastating condition estimated to affect around two women per 1,000 births. He called Clancy “a darn good mother” and argued that she received “lousy” medical care when she sought help for her deteriorating mental state. She was in “the depths of despair” when she killer her children, he argued, and was compelled to kill them and herself by a persistent male voice during a spell of psychosis.Prosecutors, meanwhile, argued that Clancy “deliberately and meticulously” killed her children, and acted “intentionally, rationally, and swiftly”. Prosecutors acknowledged Clancy’s mental health struggles but in its closing statement argued that Clancy was a “functioning mom” who knew “right and wrong”. The prosecution pointed to the medical resources and treatment available to her, and also downplayed the severity of Clancy’s suicide attempt. She put a level of planning into the killings that indicates she was not psychotic, they argued. Continue reading...

points.title: JD Vance accused of ‘gaslighting’ after saying he is ‘skeptical’ US struck Iranian wedding | First Thing
points.content: Vice-president’s claim US-Iran conflict is not war draws ridicule from Democrat Ro Khanna. Plus, iconic feminist Gloria Steinem dies aged 92Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up hereGood morning. The US vice-president, JD Vance, has responded to claims that an American strike was responsible for killing four people, including a child, at a wedding celebration in southern Iran by saying that “sometimes things happen”. The deaths were reported by the Iranian Red Crescent, which operates independently of Tehran and is treated by most international monitors as a credible source on casualty figures.In a further comment, described by the congressman Ro Khanna, a Democrat from California, as “gaslighting”, the vice-president said the conflict between the US and Iran, which has stretched into a seventh month and caused the deaths of 18 US service members, was not presently “a war”. Iranian authorities have put the overall death toll from US and Israeli strikes in the thousands, figures outside observers, including US-based monitoring groups, have broadly corroborated.What did Vance say? At a White House press briefing he said: “I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far, so I’m extremely skeptical of this. What I can say with 100% confidence is that, unlike the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the US never targets civilians in combat. We never will do that. We never have done that, and unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen”. Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to blow up Iran’s civilian infrastructure.What is happening with US military leadership? Trump on Thursday named Adam Telle as the acting army secretary after the departure of Daniel Driscoll amid widespread reports of tensions with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. Telle is currently the assistant secretary of the army for civil works.What has the House decided about university boycotts of Israel? The House has passed a Republican-backed bill that would penalize universities that participate in boycotts of Israel. “This legislation is about a simple principle: our colleges and universities should not discriminate against Israel,” said Tim Walberg, the Republican chair of the House education committee. Thirty three Democrats broke with the rest of their party to vote in favor. It now goes to the Senate for consideration. Continue reading...

points.title: ‘They disturb the game’: how betting fans are taking over tennis courts
points.content: Jeering and heckling are increasingly commonplace, even at grand slams, as spectators try to influence matchesMidway through the first week of the US Open a couple of years ago, Jiri Lehecka’s attempts to find his form were disrupted by incessant taunting from a spectator close by. “There was a guy who sat just behind my bench on a smaller court, court four, and he was talking to me basically for the first three sets, like non-stop,” Lehecka says. “He was talking to me like: ‘You can’t do it. You are tired. He’s better than you are.’”Lehecka maintained his composure and closed out the match, but even as he focused on navigating the intense stress of competition, he believed he understood this spectator’s motivations. The spectator, he thinks, was not there just to cheer for his favourite player: he was a bettor who had put money on Lehecka to lose. He had entered court four solely to influence the outcome of the match. Continue reading...

points.title: Stanford scientists discover a seafood that can reverse signs of aging
points.content: A substance found in edible sea squirts appeared to reverse several signs of aging in older mice. Plasmalogen supplements improved memory and learning, strengthened connections between brain cells, reduced inflammation, and even helped the mice grow thicker, darker hair. Researchers believe the compounds may encourage brain regeneration and protect aging synapses.

points.title: New injectable treatment helps the brain rebuild after stroke
points.content: Duke researchers developed an injectable scaffold that helped stroke-damaged brains grow new blood vessels, support nerve regrowth, and recover movement in mice. The treatment appears to work partly by recruiting the body’s own immune cells, including neutrophils that may switch from damaging to helpful under the right conditions.

points.title: Extreme drought now covers 44% of Puerto Rico
points.content: Puerto Rico’s normally rainy season has instead brought a severe and fast-growing drought. By August 25, three-quarters of the territory was in at least moderate drought, with extreme drought covering 44 percent and some areas receiving less than 20 percent of their usual rainfall. Water shortages have forced rationing, while farmers are losing crops and ranchers are running low on hay. The situation has become serious enough to trigger both local and federal disaster declarations.

points.title: Deep beneath Mars, scientists find a vast hidden magma system
points.content: Deep beneath Mars, scientists have found evidence of enormous magmatic systems once thought to require Earth-like plate tectonics. Seismic measurements suggest molten rock repeatedly evolved and recycled itself through the Martian crust, potentially across hundreds or thousands of kilometers. The discovery challenges long-held ideas about how complex planetary crusts form.

points.title: MIT turns bacteria into living transistors

One day, these biological computers could coat plant roots or leaves, detecting environmental threats and automatically triggering defenses.

points.title: Plants may be evolving the wrong traits for a warming world
points.content: Morning glories may be getting caught in an evolutionary tug-of-war between surviving climate change and attracting increasingly scarce pollinators. Over just nine years, researchers found that the plants’ rate of adaptation plunged by 96%, even though they still had plenty of genetic diversity to evolve.

points.title: Dying radio galaxies fade faster than scientists expected
points.content: Astronomers have identified a surprisingly young population of fading radio galaxies whose supermassive black holes have already switched off their powerful jets. The confirmed remnants range from about 8 to 42 million years old, suggesting many may disappear from view much faster than previously recognized. More distant remnants also seem to fade especially quickly, helping explain why they have been so difficult to detect.

points.title: How much does Donald Trump care about winning the midterms? Apparently, not much at all | Jonathan Freedland
points.content: Such is the US president’s narcissism that he would see a Democratic victory as proof that he’s indispensable – meanwhile, his every decision spells calamity for votersWhat is Donald Trump playing at? If it’s true that the best way of understanding the behaviour of an organisation is to assume it’s controlled by a secret cabal of its enemies, perhaps that same logic extends to the current conduct of the president of the United States. Maybe he secretly wants Republicans to lose the looming midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in the US for the next two years and for which the first postal ballots were sent out today.That’s not as mad a theory as it sounds. Indeed, there are at least two reasons why Trump might either be unbothered by Republican defeat in November or even covertly desire it. We’ll come to those, but let’s start with a pattern of behaviour that is hard to explain as anything other than calculated self-sabotage.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

points.title: USL and players ratify new CBA, raising salaries and introducing 12-month deals
points.content: New pact includes terms for first-division USL PremierBase pay for Championship grows from $31k to $42kAgreement runs through the 2030 seasonThe United Soccer League and USL Players Association announced the ratification of a new collective bargaining agreement for two levels of the organization’s pyramid on Friday, with fresh terms taking effect immediately and running through 2030. The new pact include a second agreement for the second-division USL Championship as well as the first set of terms for the upcoming USL Premier, a first-division sanctioned league scheduled to lauch in 2028.Among the headline items of the deals is the introduction of 12-month contracts for players, a codified first in the US lower divisions. The first USL CBAs worked to standardize 10-month contracts; before then, clubs varied in their commitments to players. Championship players will earn a base compensation (which includes housing) of $42,000 in 2026 – up from $31,000 – with that floor increasing annually over the term of the agreement. points.title: Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash is built for agents, while its Cyber twin hunts vulnerabilities
points.content: Google keeps cranking out Flash models: the company on Wednesday announced two versions of a new 3.8 Flash. The variants include a standard Flash, a “workhorse” model for agentic tasks, software development, and multi-step reasoning, and Flash Cyber optimized for vulnerability detection and mitigation.Google CEO Sundar Pichai said in an X post that 3.8 Flash delivers “significant leaps” from 3.7 Flash across software engineering, agentic tasks, and multi-step reasoning. For instance, it outperformed many large frontier models on the DeepSWE coding benchmark, at far lower cost. Meanwhile, Flash Cyber is the company’s “most capable” cybersecurity model, Pichai said; it also matches frontier-level performance when it comes to discovering vulnerabilities and patching them at scale. The model achieved 86.2% on the CyberGym cybersecurity benchmark and 47.2% on CWE-Bench, which evaluates AI patching abilities. In an internal Google benchmark, the model achieved a more than 70% success rate discovering vulnerabilities across 20 programming languages, Pichai said. 3.8 is Google’s third Flash release in six weeks and comes quickly on the heels of version 3.7. 3.8 working harder with greater diligence 3.8 Flash is available now in Gemini Enterprise; devs can try it out in the Gemini API via Google AI Studio, Google Antigravity, Android Studio, or generate UIs in Stitch. It is priced at $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens — the same introductory pricing as Gemini 3.7 Flash — and users can customize and adjust model effort levels based on their needs around quality, cost, and latency. For instance, when compute efficiency is a priority, they can adjust to lower token overhead, or simply continue working with 3.7 Flash, which is “fully supported for efficiency-first workloads,” Google senior product director Tulsee Doshi and Gemini security lead Raluca Ada Popa wrote in a blog post. “3.8 Flash works harder,” exhibiting “greater diligence” with complex tasks like executing extra reasoning steps, although at times it may use more tokens to maximize performance, Doshi and Popa note. The model has a 1M-token input window and a 64K-token output limit, and can ingest text as well as images, audio, video, and PDF files. 3.8 Flash was evaluated across numerous benchmarks testing coding, multimodal capabilities, computer use, long-context and knowledge work, and scientific reasoning. Google says it also does well in specialized knowledge domains requiring more in-depth analysis and reporting. For instance, the model outperformed its predecessor and other frontier models on benchmarks like Vals Finance Agent V2 for finance, and Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark for law; it also scored 54.9% on Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE)-Verified, reflecting its ability to take on multi-step reasoning tasks across subjects like math, science, and humanities. In one example shared by Google, Gemini 3.8 Flash built a game with a simple prompt using looping techniques in Google’s Antigravity platform. The game uses puzzles, storytelling that changes based on the environment, and images and textures from Nano Banana to create a 3D experience (in this case a wizard navigating a castle). In other instances, the model created a fully-functional DOS version of Google Maps featuring interactive locations, directions, and street views; a 3D visualizer that automatically decomposed devices into layers for inspection with a slider capability; and a topographic map of famous geographical sites based on real datasets from the U.S. Geological Survey, complete with real-time cross-sections, 2D projections, and scientific explanations. According to Arena.ai, 3.8 Flash landed at No. 14 in Agent Arena, ranking above DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and showed a significant jump over Gemini 3.7 Flash (which sits all the way down at No. 32). It debuted at No. 7 in Text Arena, ahead of Claude Opus 5 and Gemini 3.7 Flash. It improved over 3.7 Flash in several areas: multi-turn requests, writing, literature, and language, longer queries, hard prompts, coding, instruction following, software and IT services, and business, management and financial ops. Flash Cyber is already securing Google's codeFlash Cyber is initially being rolled out to “trusted defenders” through Google’s Fairwind Program, which prioritizes government authorities, critical-infrastructure operators, and other partners looking for advanced cyber defense capabilities. Organizations can apply for access. Google says the model version has undergone “rigorous training” in the cybersecurity domain and represents a “significant leap in prompt injection robustness.” It is particularly adept at autonomous vulnerability discovery — at least, based on internal Gemini benchmarks — and automated patching. It is also very good at coding, Popa said in a video. The goal was to equip defenders with expert-level capabilities to give them a leg up over threat actors (whether malicious, fellow AI agents, or human hackers). “We have invested in vulnerability fixing from the start, and prioritized it over offensive capabilities like exploitation,” Doshi and Popa explain. The model ships a more permissive set of mitigations for cybersecurity safeguards — which is why, for now, it is only being shared with limited partners — and safeguards against misuse in cyber offense and areas like chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN).Google is already using 3.8 Flash Cyber to secure its own code; it produced 2.6 times more correct patches in Chrome vulnerabilities versus much larger commercial models. Wiz — which Google acquired earlier this year at a historic $32 billion — reported that 3.8 Flash Cyber had 7.5% to 9.7% higher recall of real-world vulnerabilities on an internal penetration testing benchmark at 2.3 to 5.2 times lower cost than leading frontier models. Similarly, Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research found a critical foundational vulnerability in less than 2 hours with 3.8 Flash Cyber. Typically, that research and discovery would take months, Google claims. AI agents are “incredibly skilled” at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, Popa said. Scanning large codebases with big AI models is expensive, and defenders are overwhelmed. “In cybersecurity, attackers need only find one significant flaw over millions of lines of code. Defenders have to remove every one of those flaws to be able to defend against attackers.” Doug Turner, engineering director for Chrome, described a “vulnerability apocalypse” in recent months due to generative AI. “Simply overnight, we saw a hockey stick increase in the number of software vulnerabilities reported through our vulnerability research program,” he said in a video. One interesting vulnerability 3.8 Flash Cyber discovered had been in Chromium and Chrome for 13 years, he explained. It was a “very subtle bug” that dozens, if not hundreds, of engineers looked at but never flagged. “Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber is going to allow us to create better suggested fixes so that developers’ lives can get a lot easier.”

points.title: Gloria Steinem personified America’s feminist movement | Moira Donegan
points.content: The activist made the movement mainstream – and became a receptacle for its hopes and disappointmentsGloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist campaigner, dies aged 92‘We badly need to raise our boys more like our girls’: Gloria Steinem – a life in quotesBy the time she died on Wednesday, at 92 years old at her home in New York, Gloria Steinem was synonymous with feminism, a kind of human mascot for the movement. So it can be easy to forget that when she was born, feminism was over. It was something that had been faddish years before, among women who were now old ladies; something that seemed, in retrospect, like it might have been a bit overwrought and out of touch. To the girl Gloria Steinem, growing up in Ohio in the 1930s and 40s, the suffrage movement that had gained women the right to vote less than two decades prior probably seemed remote – especially to a girl like her, growing up itinerant and poor under the care of a single mother who was plagued by a violent and debilitating mental illness. You might say that growing up, Steinem had worries that were more immediate than the status of women.But experience has a way of radicalizing women about their own gendered condition. Steinem attended Smith, and her education opened up previously unhoped for possibilities. En route to a postgraduate fellowship in India in 1957, when she was in her early 20s, she had an illegal abortion in London. Later, in 1969, while she was working as a journalist for New York magazine, she attended an “abortion speak-out” put on by a group of radical women from the emergent fringe of what was then called the Women’s Liberation movement.
